name: Sun-protective white face coating

lead: People have long covered the face with pale mineral pastes to keep the sun off the skin. Preventing sunburn, tanning and sunspots helps preserve an even complexion and slows visible photoageing.

Zinc oxide, the usual white ingredient, is a broad-spectrum UV filter that also reads as white pigment, which is why thick layers look chalky. Traditional pastes such as thanaka in Myanmar are part of the same family of practices.

paras: The coating is spread over the face as a paste, cream or powder, with thicker, more opaque layers for outdoor sport and finer modern mineral formulas for daily wear. Many people layer it over or in place of chemical sunscreens, and some blend it with tinted products to reduce the white cast.

Zinc oxide is generally described as non-irritating and non-comedogenic, with a small amount of zinc absorbed through skin [2]. The main drawback is cosmetic: thick opaque layers look white. Historical or homemade coatings that use other minerals can differ in safety from regulated sunscreens.

angle.text: The coating protects skin from UV, and avoiding sun damage keeps the complexion more even over time. Some users apply it deliberately visible for outdoor activity, others choose finer tinted versions.

lead: A sun-protective white face coating is a pale, opaque layer applied to the face to block sunlight. It helps appearance by reducing sunburn, uneven tanning and the pigment changes associated with accumulated sun exposure.

Zinc oxide paste has been used on skin for a very long time, and traditional sun-protective pastes include borak (Sama-Bajau people), thanaka (Myanmar) and masonjoany (Madagascar, since the 18th century) [1]. Accounts of ancient Egyptian protection mention extracts of rice, jasmine and lupine [1]. Ancient Greeks used olive oil [1].

Today mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide and/or titanium dioxide, and the US FDA recognised only these two as generally recognised as safe and effective as of 2021 [1]. Zinc oxide is a broad-spectrum UVA and UVB filter, and nanoparticle forms avoid leaving a white cast [2].
infobox: Zinc oxide recognised as safe and effective sunscreen ingredient [1]

paras: The practice covers any pale, opaque topical coating used to shield the face from sun, from traditional pastes to modern high-zinc products. Pure zinc oxide is a white powder widely used as a pigment, so thick layers show clearly on the skin [2].

Zinc oxide paste has been used for skin protection for thousands of years, and zinc oxide salves appear in historical medical texts including the Charaka Samhita and the writings of Dioscorides [1][2]. Commercial sunscreens developed in the twentieth century: an Australian chemist produced a tannic acid product in 1932, L'Oreal released a sunscreen in 1936, and SPF was introduced in 1974 [1].

Zinc oxide absorbs UVA and UVB light and is photostable; mineral sunscreens also reflect and scatter some UV [1][2]. Nanoparticle zinc oxide scatters little visible light, leaving less white cast, and the particles remain in the outermost skin layer [2].

Zinc oxide is considered non-irritating, non-allergenic and non-comedogenic, though a small amount of zinc is absorbed [2]. The US FDA lists it as generally recognised as safe as a food additive, and inhaling high concentrations of its fumes can cause metal fume fever [2].
